steps.say: Brain tangles of abnormal vessels are graded by size, by whether they sit in critical brain, and by how they drain. Small surface tangles are low-scoring and large deep ones are high-scoring. That single number predicts the risk of removing them.
steps.tx: The **Spetzler-Martin grade** (AVM risk score) sums size below **3 cm** (three centimetres) as **1** (one), **3 to 6 cm** (three to six centimetres) as **2** (two) and above **6 cm** (six centimetres) as **3** (three), plus **1** (one) each for **eloquent location** (critical brain area) and **deep venous drainage** (deep vein outflow). Totals give grades **1 to 5** (one to five), with **6** (six) reserved for inoperable lesions.

vis.alt: Lateral cerebral angiogram revealing a large cerebral arteriovenous malformation (AVM) with a prominent nidus, dilated feeding arteries and enlarged, tortuous draining veins, including a large venous varix.
vis.caption: Large AVM nidus with feeding arteries and draining veins on angiogram. Credit: Illustration by Royonx, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

steps.say: Low-grade tangles are removed with high cure rates and low harm. Mid-grade ones need a mix of surgery, radiation and embolisation planned together. High-grade tangles are usually left alone unless they have already burst and threaten life.
steps.tx: **Grade I and II** (grades one and two) tangles are surgical lesions with high cure and low morbidity, grade **3** (three) is borderline **multimodality** (combined treatments) territory, and grades **4 and 5** (four and five) are usually watched. A **ruptured AVM** (burst tangle) with life-threatening haematoma breaks the rule, since the clot already did the damage surgery fears.

steps.say: For tangles found by chance that have never bled, a landmark trial settled the argument. Pills and watchful waiting beat intervention at five years. Incidental tangles are therefore observed, while burst ones are treated.
steps.tx: **ARUBA** (unruptured AVM trial) randomised unruptured AVMs and found **medical management** (observation without intervention) superior to intervention at **5 years** (five years). Incidental **unruptured AVM** (never-bled tangle) malformations are therefore generally observed, while ruptured ones are treated, since operating on a quiet lesion risks what nature might never do.

steps.say: Every year, two to four in a hundred tangles burst, and some features raise the odds. A previous bleed, a deep or back-of-head position and pouches on the feeding arteries all mark higher risk. Aneurysms on the feeders are closed first when they bleed.
steps.tx: Annual **rupture risk** (yearly burst chance) is **2 to 4 percent** (two to four percent), rising with **prior rupture** (previous bleed), deep or posterior fossa location and associated **flow aneurysms** (feeder pouches). Such aneurysms are secured first when they bleed, since they burst more readily than the tangle itself and their closure calms the whole malformation.

steps.say: Deep tangles that surgery cannot reach are treated with focused radiation beams. The tangle closes slowly over two to five years, and it can still bleed during the wait. Small compact knots are the ones that close best with this approach.
steps.tx: **Radiosurgery** (focused radiation beams) obliterates deep or eloquent AVMs over **2 to 5 years** (two to five years), with a **latency period** (waiting-years bleed risk) during closure. It suits lesions below **3 cm** (three centimetres) with a compact **nidus** (central knot), where beams can cover the whole tangle without injuring surrounding brain.

steps.say: Glue-like liquid delivered through a microcatheter can shrink a tangle before surgery or radiation, and it cures only tiny selected knots alone. Sessions are staged because closing too much at once floods normal brain with blood. That flooding injury is the complication surgeons fear most.
steps.tx: Glue embolisation with **Onyx embolisation** (liquid embolic injection) finishes off only tiny chosen knots on its own; its usual job is shrinking bigger tangles ahead of surgery or radiosurgery. Treatment runs in **staged sessions** (planned stepwise sittings) to avoid normal **perfusion pressure breakthrough** (flood injury to normal brain), where sudden rerouting of blood swells and bleeds healthy tissue.

vis.alt: Diagram illustrating AVM embolisation, showing a microcatheter delivering liquid embolic agent into the AVM nidus, effectively casting the malformation and its shunts.
vis.caption: Microcatheter casting the AVM nidus with liquid embolic before surgery. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Seizures from an accessible surface tangle can themselves justify an operation. Removing the knot to stop fits makes sense when the cortex nearby handles no critical function. Deep silent tangles stay unoperated because the cure would cost more than the seizures.
steps.tx: When fits come from a reachable surface tangle lying beside but outside critical cortex, removing the knot to stop the epilepsy can be justified. A **lesionectomy** (knot removal) suits surface tangles clear of critical **eloquent cortex** (speech and movement brain) as treatment for **AVM epilepsy** (tangle-driven fits), while deep asymptomatic lesions stay observed.

steps.say: Some patients grow many tangles as part of an inherited vessel disease, with nosebleeds and spots on the lips. Their lungs may hide abnormal connections that throw clots to the brain. Whole families need screening once the pattern is recognised.
steps.tx: Hereditary haemorrhagic **telangiectasia** (inherited vessel-spot disease) and Wyburn-Mason patterns with multiple AVMs need **family screening** (relative testing) plus lung evaluation. A **pulmonary AVM** (lung short-circuit) lets clots reach the brain, causing abscess and stroke, so affected families are screened for lung shunts as well as brain lesions.
